newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Racial abuse on rise say Chinese Australians.
newsitem.headline: Racial abuse on rise say Chinese Australians.

text.p: Racial abuse against Chinese Australians has doubled, with many being spat at or physically threatened, since independent politican Pauline Hanson sparked a xenophobic race debate, according to a newspaper survey.
The survey in the daily Sing Tao, Australia's largest Chinese language newspaper, released on Wednesday found physical, written and verbal abuse had risen in the past month.

"We had heard of anecdotal reports of more abuse, but the survey showed it had doubled since the speech," said Thiam Ang, president of the Chinese Australian Forum, referring to Hanson's claim that Australia is being swamped by Asians.
"I think it is shameful that law abiding citizens of this country are being attacked because of their appearance. It is a disgraceful thing," Ang told Reuters.
More than 1,000 people responded to the Chinese Australian Forum questionaire in Sing Tao in late October, which asked if, when, and how people had been abused.

One third of respondents, 345 people, said they had experienced abuse before Hanson initiated the race debate in a maiden parliamentary speech on October 12. But 764 people said they had been victimised since the speech.
Sing Tao has a daily circulation of about 25,000.
But in a nationally televised chat-show on Wednesday, Prime Minister John Howard defended Australia as a tolerant society.
"I think that Australians are tolerant," Howard said.
"Not all of them -- there are bigots in the Australian community, but compared with other nations we have an incredible record of decency and tolerance," Howard said.

The Chinese newspaper survey asked people to categorise their abuse as physical, written, verbal or whether they had been spat at. "We had heard a lot of reports that people were being spaton and for Chinese it is a terrible thing. In the Chinese culture it means you are a mongrel dog," Ang said.
The survey found almost a three-fold increase, from 25 to 79, in the number of Chinese Australians being spat on.

The greatest increase in racial abuse was verbal, from 299 to 670. Physical abuse, such as families being pushed around in the street, increased from 40 to 95, while written abuse, such as threatening letters rose from 23 to 47.
"One of the aims of our organisation is to integrate Chinese into Australian society, but this has put us back," Ang said.
The Chinese Australian Forum criticised Howard, saying his failure to end the race debate showed a lack of leadership, a view shared by political analysts and other ethnic groups.
"I think he (Howard) should change his tact and stand up and protect those Australians being hurt -- call on people to stop this abuse," Ang said.
Howard has opposed racial intolerance and not agreed with Hanson, but he has championed her right to freedom of speech.

Popular support for Hanson, who has said incorrectly said Asians are swamping Australia and has called for a halt to Asian immigration, has been unexpectedly strong with one opinion poll finding 71 percent of voters thought immigration was too high.
Hanson, a fish-and-chip shop owner, on Wednesday defended her views, saying: "I am not a redneck, I am not a racist and I won't be called one".
"It's not that I said I didn't like Asians, I said I wanted balance restored in this country," Hanson said during the recording of a cable telvision panel show.
